2:04 · Most of these microscopic roommates are harmless.

2:07 · Just freeloaders, basically.

2:10 · But one can cause real trouble.

2:13 · The house dust mite.

2:15 · This is like the roommate who leaves his crap around and makes you sick.

2:19 · Dust mites don’t bite people. They don’t need to.

2:22 · We feed them constantly.

2:25 · Skin flakes are hard to digest.

2:28 · It’s like eating hair …

2:29 · or feathers.

2:31 · So dust mites have powerful digestive enzymes to break the skin down.

2:36 · Those enzymes turn up in dust mite poop.

2:39 · And let’s just say you really don’t want to know how much dust mite poop is in your house.

2:44 · When people breathe dust, they breathe in the poop – and the enzymes, too … which irritate the lungs and can aggravate asthma, especially in kids.

2:54 · Like us humans, dust mites haven’t always lived inside either.

2:59 · These tiny relatives of spiders and scorpions once lived in birds’ nests.

3:04 · But then, some intrepid dust mites made the jump …

3:08 · from birds’ homes to ours.

3:10 · And as our society thrived and grew, so did theirs.

3:16 · If you like this video, please hit the like and subscribe buttons.

3:19 · It really helps us reach more people, and we truly appreciate your support!

Bed bugs

3:24 · These bed bugs are after your blood and they go for it while you’re sleeping.

3:29 · Keep watching to see how researchers stop them dead in their tracks.

3:35 · Good night, sleep tight, don’t let the … OK, you know where this is going.

3:41 · [ominous music] Lured in by our breath, bed bugs come for us when we’re most vulnerable.

3:51 · In dreamland, we’re oblivious …

3:54 · … to bed bug chow time.

3:58 · You won’t even feel it.

4:00 · It’s a quick meal. Just a few minutes.

4:03 · But it’s a filling one.

4:10 · Stuffed with blood, it scurries to a nearby cranny.

4:14 · The seam of your mattress … … or behind a baseboard.

4:22 · There, they get to work growing their families.

4:28 · Until you get … You can recognize them by their signature work of art.

4:47 · These tiny splotches.

4:50 · It’s the digested blood they leave behind.

4:54 · In the 1950s, we made bed bugs retreat with DDT.

5:00 · But some became resistant and now they’re back.

5:08 · We help them spread – in our clothes or luggage – when we travel around.

5:15 · You can kill them with other insecticides or heat, but their game of hide-and-seek makes it tricky.

5:22 · Turns out, there might be another way to stop them in their tracks.

5:27 · Watch this.

5:29 · It’s just taking a stroll and … Gotcha!

5:34 · Its foot is stuck.

5:36 · This bean leaf can incapacitate the bloodsuckers.

5:42 · People in the Balkans discovered that years ago and would spread the leaves around their beds as a trap.

5:48 · The leaf’s surface is covered in these tiny hooked hairs called trichomes.

6:02 · They pierce right through the bed bug’s feet, impaling their soft joints.

6:16 · Many bean plants – like kidney and green beans – developed the hooks to defend against aphids and other plant-eating pests.

6:25 · But it just so happens to work on our bloodthirsty pest too.

6:35 · Biologist and engineer Catherine Loudon is trying to copy the plant at the University of California, Irvine.

6:43 · She’s creating a synthetic material that can pierce bed bug feet just like bean leaves do.

6:52 · It’s not quite as effective as a real bean leaf, but she’s working on it.

7:05 · In the meantime, bed bugs are still a step ahead. So keep an eye out.

7:12 · Spot them early and maybe you can get them before they get you.

Termites

7:19 · Termites can infiltrate your home without being seen, and the results can be catastrophic.

7:25 · But these tiny homewreckers wouldn’t be able to do so much damage without the help of special microorganisms hidden in their gut.

7:36 · That lump on the side of this tree in the Amazon?

7:39 · It’s packed with termites. In the rainforest, that’s a good thing.

7:45 · They break down wood into stuff other creatures can eat.

7:48 · But inside our homes, termites are pests. They cost us billions of dollars of damage every year.

7:55 · Take these dampwood termites that live on the cool California coast.

7:59 · They eat wood that’s wet or decayed, maybe from a leak in your house.

8:05 · Slowly, but surely, they gnaw and scrape away.

8:10 · What comes out the other end isn’t waste.

8:16 · It serves as a kind of mortar.

8:20 · And dried poop pellets make perfect building blocks for their nests.

8:25 · In other words, they’re turning your house into theirs.

8:29 · What’s amazing is that they can digest wood, which is so hard, and get nutrients out of it.

8:35 · We certainly can’t do that.

8:37 · Termites are one of the only animals that can.

8:40 · It turns out they don’t do this alone.

8:43 · Researchers are looking inside termites to figure out who’s actually responsible for this feat.

8:49 · At the Exploratorium, in San Francisco, museum biologists give the insect a little puff of carbon dioxide.

8:57 · When it’s nice and relaxed, the termite poops itself.

9:03 · Under the microscope, multitudes appear.

9:07 · Hundreds of species of microbes live packed inside a termite’s gut, about one one-thousandth of a teaspoon.

9:14 · This big one is called Trichonympha.

9:17 · It’s not an animal, plant or fungus. It’s a protist.

9:21 · Watch it move with the help of its flagella.

9:26 · Protists like Trichonympha are essential for termites to turn the wood into a source of energy.

9:31 · They do this by fermenting the wood, much the same way a brewer turns grain into beer.

9:38 · Something else is hidden deep in the termite’s gut.

9:41 · A powerful bacterium that combines nitrogen from the air and calories from the wood to make protein.

9:48 · That’s like turning a potato into a steak.

9:51 · Termites can’t live without their microbes.

9:53 · And many of these microbes can’t live outside the termite.

9:57 · So what if we used the microbes against their hosts?

10:01 · Right now, when we want to get rid of termites, we fumigate our houses with poison.

10:08 · But maybe we could just kill the protists instead.

10:11 · Louisiana State University entomologists are engineering a gut bacterium to kill gut protists.

10:18 · They’d sneak the bacteria into the termite colony on something the termites would eat.

10:24 · The bacteria would kill the protists that help the termites digest wood, leaving them surrounded by food but starving.

10:34 · If you love learning about wildlife, subscribe to our weekly newsletter. It’s free!

10:39 · Link in the description.

Drain flies

10:42 · These cuties are experts in making their way into your house through some secret and slimy passageways.

10:50 · Check it out.

10:54 · Ever wonder where those little insects crawling around your bathroom came from?

11:00 · Bad news: your drain.

11:05 · With all that fluffy hair, it looks like a tiny moth.

11:12 · And some do call it a moth fly.

11:15 · But a fly it is.

11:18 · A drain fly.

11:20 · It’s called Clogmia – how appropriate.

11:24 · It grew up over several weeks, out of sight, among things you thought you’d washed away.

11:33 · Drain flies sneak in from the outside, through a crack in an old pipe, for example, to sip some water they sensed with this long mustache – their maxillary palps.

11:47 · And here, on the plentiful gunk in your pipes, they’ll grow a family.

11:52 · Welcome, little one!

11:54 · The larva is the length of an eyelash.

11:58 · That gunk it lives in? Those are bits of you: hair, saliva and food.

12:04 · They make a nice meal for bacteria and fungi, which form this dark, living slime called a biofilm.

12:13 · This is what the larvae feed on.

12:17 · It also keeps them well moisturized.

12:21 · If the larva ends up submerged, it can still chow down.

12:27 · It sweeps slime particles out of the water with a hairy mouthpart called the labrum.

12:37 · And rakes them in with its mandibles.

12:44 · Underwater, it breathes with a bubble on its backside that it collected at the surface.

12:52 · This allows it to venture through deep pools in your pipes.

12:56 · When larvae, or the more grown-up pupae, like this guy here, end up in a toilet bowl, it can be a shock.

13:06 · You might think the squigglers came out of you!

13:10 · Ew!

13:11 · Don’t worry – they can’t live inside us.

13:15 · And even though the drain flies in your bathroom muck around in bacteria, they don’t really spread it to humans.

13:23 · They’re not interested in landing on us. Or even leaving the bathroom.

13:27 · They’re in their happy place.

13:30 · When you wash your hands?

13:32 · They protect themselves from the water with their hairy wings.

13:37 · Each hair has ridges that trap air so the drops roll right off.

13:47 · And if they’re caught off-guard by a sudden surge, the flies skate across.

13:56 · But they’re not invincible.

13:59 · When they get trapped underwater long enough, they can drown.

14:06 · If you find you really need to get rid of them, drain cleaner helps, but it won’t keep them away forever.

14:13 · There will always be some slime left behind, deep in your pipes, that could attract the flies again.

14:21 · So, if they want it, why not let ‘em have it?

Cockroaches

14:26 · Are cockroaches – those disgusting disease-spreading roommates – good for anything at all?

14:32 · [hitting wood] [hitting floor] Scientists think their super-strength might teach us some tricks that could someday save lives.

14:41 · The American cockroach is one of the fastest insects on the planet.

14:47 · It can run up to 3.4 miles per hour.

14:51 · That’d be like a human knocking out eight marathons over their lunch break.

14:58 · It uses hooks, called tarsal claws, to flip over ledges.

15:02 · [cymbal ta-da] [cymbal ta-da] And not even a wall can stop it.

15:21 · Better to keep up the momentum and figure it out as you go.

15:28 · The roach is both tough and flexible.

15:32 · Its exoskeleton isn’t one large piece of armor, but many shield-like plates made of a tough material called chitin.

15:42 · They’re held together by lots of pliable joints.

15:46 · And they use all those bendy joints to fold up, origami-style, and push through impossibly small cracks … … like that gap you never knew existed in your kitchen cupboard.

16:02 · The cockroach can army-crawl through a space a quarter of its normal standing height.

16:09 · That’s one reason it’s so good at surviving your thwack.

16:15 · So how much pressure can the cockroach take?

16:19 · Scientists at UC Berkeley found it can withstand a thwack …

16:24 · … equivalent to 900 times its body weight … … and walk away unscathed.

16:32 · Why are researchers so interested in all this?

16:35 · They think the roach, despite its ability to make us sick, can teach us to save lives.

16:43 · One of those researchers is now building robots the size of insects to squeeze into places you and I cannot.

16:52 · Like piles of rubble left by major earthquakes or hurricanes.

17:00 · And maybe down the line, much smaller versions of these robots could even enter our bodies to perform life-saving tasks.

17:11 · On the one hand, we want to keep these creatures out …

17:14 · by sealing cracks, caulking windows and storing food in airtight containers.

17:20 · But we also want to learn from them.

17:24 · The cockroach teaches us that the key to overcoming adversity isn’t just toughness.

17:30 · It’s also flexibility.

A NASA study explains how to purify air with house plants

Quartz, 12 01, 2017

Video (3:13)
Description

How do houseplants clean the air? A 1989 NASA study explains exactly how plants remove toxins from air by trapping them in their leaves, soil, and roots, and which houseplants clean air the best.

The study was designed to test air purification systems for the space station.

https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19930073077.pdf

And if you want to buy the last plant? It’s scientific name is Sansevieria laurentii, but common names are both snake plant and mother in law’s tongue.

The 1989 NASA study

0:00 · You’ve probably heard plants can improve your air quality.

0:02 · Just about every paper on the subject, [and I mean literally all of them,] are based on a 1989 NASA study and a follow up by the lead scientist.

NASA plant experiment

0:19 · The scientists collected plants and put them in chambers, then pumped in harmful chemicals like these: After 24 hours, they tested the air quality in each chamber.

0:33 · Some plants were able to remove up to 90% of the harmful chemicals.

0:37 · So which plants were the most effective?

0:40 · NASA scientists tested familiar ones.

0:42 · “All the plants they have in their list are just very common house plants.

0:46 · This is Dr Dennis Stevenson, Vice President for science at the New York Botanical Garden.

0:53 · “I think they picked them because they were looking at things that people would have in their environments.

0:58 · As opposed to some exotic, weird tropical plant that nobody knows anything about.”

1:04 · All of these plants are excellent at getting rid of harmful indoor carcinogens.

How plants filter air

1:15 · Here’s how it works: Plants take in the harmful gasses out of the atmosphere and sequester them in their roots and cells.

1:23 · Some of these chemicals are broken down by fungi in the soil and others are stored in the plant.

1:28 · So what about things like…smoke, that might be in your apartment via cigarettes.

1:33 · Or you know…other types of smoke.

1:37 · “Well I would say, they take up stuff in the atmosphere so theoretically they should take up any kind of smoke that’s in your apartment in a certain sense, right.

1:50 · I don’t really know, but I think if one did those tests that probably one would find a positive correlation with that.”

Best plants for cleaner air

2:01 · Of all of the plants NASA mentioned in its study these three have the best surface area to chemical removal ratio.

2:13 · But keep in mind that a gerbera daisy will never get as big as a lady palm, and the more plant you have, the more harmful chemicals that you can remove.

2:22 · “ A big leaf plant is probably, potentially able to exchange more things with the air you know than something with little needle leaves.”

2:32 · And for those lacking a green thumb?

2:35 · “I’ll tell you, the one in there that’s probably the hardest to kill is the sansevieria, the mother in law’s tongue.”

2:43 · It scores high on removing chemicals and only needs low light.

A public housing project where healthy living is the foundation

Description

In downtown Denver, a recently built public housing project is designed to foster healthy living, with access to nutritious food, access to doctors and ease of exercise and public transportation. Jeffrey Brown reports.

0:25 · JEFFREY BROWN: Her change in behavior didn’t happen by accident.

0:28 · Four years ago, here in downtown Denver, Taylor joined an experiment in making healthy living part of the design and daily life of a public housing project.

2:34 · Already, Mariposa is becoming a model for rethinking public housing.

3:24 · JEFFREY BROWN: Trejo now has a job at one of Denver’s top restaurants, and plans to operate his own food truck soon.

3:30 · ANGELA RODRIGUEZ, Denver: Are you looking forward to helping me grow some fruits and vegetables?

3:36 · JEFFREY BROWN: Angela Rodriguez, a single mother of two teens, dreams of one day buying her own home.

3:42 · She has a full-time job at a nearby community college, but Denver’s booming housing market makes ownership difficult.

3:50 · She lives in a subsidized town home at Mariposa, which she says is very different from the old-style projects she grew up in nearby.

3:57 · ANGELA RODRIGUEZ: As a new style of public housing, it did take me a little bit of time for the adjustment.

4:03 · When new tenants are mingling with other tenants that come from different walks of life, it’s helping us to develop into new perspectives of modern living.

4:13 · JEFFREY BROWN: Rodriguez uses public transportation, has taken up gardening, and has fully embraced the culture of health that is promoted here.

4:22 · But is Mariposa working?

4:24 · It’s too early for definitive answers.

4:27 · According to a 2015 study by the Denver Public Health Department, about half the residents had participated in health-related activities over the previous three years.

4:38 · But the study also showed the amount of exercise residents pursued had changed little.

4:43 · Just over a third said they exercised five times a week.

4:47 · About the same amount said they exercised one to four times a week, and 26 percent said they rarely or never exercised.

4:55 · Smoking rates decreased, but only slightly, from 30 percent of residents down to 24 percent.

5:01 · And these so-called active staircases, designed with a bit of whimsy…

5:05 · ISMAEL GUERRERO: It’s a way to engage kids, and actually now the adults enjoy it.

5:09 · JEFFREY BROWN: … to lure residents away from using the elevator.

5:12 · Well, so far, they’re not having a big impact.

5:15 · THERESA MICKIEWICZ, Denver Public Health: We actually did observational counts, where we sat there and we counted people who used the stairs vs. people who used the elevator, and we compared it against a control staircase in the Mariposa redevelopment, and we found absolutely no difference.

5:32 · JEFFREY BROWN: Theresa Mickiewicz, an epidemiologist with Denver Public Health, is overseeing a study of the development.

5:38 · And while major improvements in health remain to be seen, she believes something important is happening here, and she expects the numbers to reflect that soon.

5:47 · THERESA MICKIEWICZ: While maintaining my objectivity as an evaluator, do I think that there is value in this type of project?

5:55 · I would say yes.

5:57 · Individually, these components have been shown in the evidence, in literature, to improve health outcomes.

6:04 · JEFFREY BROWN: The city of Denver is so confident in this new model, it’s about to embark on a similar development that will be three times larger than Mariposa.

6:13 · That construction is expected to begin later next year.

6:17 · For the “PBS NewsHour,” I’m Jeffrey Brown, reporting from Denver.

America’s deadliest road, explained

Vox, 11 10, 2022

Video (7:16)
Description

US road design favors speed over pedestrian safety.

Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Most American roads aren’t just unpleasant for pedestrians, they can be dangerous. Pedestrian fatalities have been rising in the past few years, and urban planners point to the way roads are designed as the culprit.

A group of urban planners identified 60 pedestrian fatality hot spots throughout the US, and a 1,000-meter corridor of US-19 in New Port Richey, Florida, topped their list. Seventeen pedestrians lost their lives along this short stretch of road in the study period of 2001 to 2016.

The fatality hot spots on the study’s list shared a lot of design characteristics. Many of them are arterial thoroughfares: roads historically built to keep high-speed traffic off of nearby residential streets. But the way US communities developed in a sprawling fashion along these roads meant these roadways also became business centers that pedestrians might need to access. The number of lanes and distances between crosswalks are among other dangerous design elements.

For this video, we went to New Port Richey to walk along US-19 and document the design characteristics identified in the study.

–

Correction - A previous version of this video featured an interview that spoke to a memorial at Main Street and US-19. Locals from the New Port Richey area brought to our attention that the interview misrepresented the memorial, which honors a young man who was killed during an accident between two cars, not a bicycle as stated in the interview. Our sincere apologies for including the misrepresentation of the victim’s story. We have edited the video to correct that error.

This is a link to a GoFundMe for the victim’s family which includes more details about the incident: https://www.gofundme.com/f/qe5jkz-funeral-expenses-for-logan-blakley

–

This video is an adaptation of Vox.com reporter Marin Cogan’s investigation of US-19:

https://www.vox.com/23178764/florida-us19-deadliest-pedestrian-fatality-crisis

Local journalists have credited Marin’s reporting for pressuring local officials to follow through on planned improvements to US-19:

https://www.tampabay.com/news/pasco/2022/09/26/deadliest-road-pasco-county-getting-millions-safety-upgrades/

The pedestrian fatality study this story is based on is below:

https://www.jtlu.org/index.php/jtlu/article/view/1825

A source for this story was Eric Dumbaugh, who authored a study on arterial roads:

https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01944360902950349

Transcript

0:00 · I’ve just arrived at the most dangerous place to be a pedestrian in the US.

0:05 · US-19 in New Port Richey, Florida on the state’s Gulf Coast.

0:10 · A group of urban planners looked at the entire US roadway network and identified 60 pedestrian fatality hotspots: 1000 meter corridors where pedestrian deaths are most common.

0:21 · And this 1000 meter stretch topped their list.

0:24 · 17 fatal crashes here in a 16 year study window.

0:28 · Pedestrian fatalities in the U.S.

0:30 · have been creeping up in the past decade thanks mostly to the way road infrastructure favors cars above all else.

0:37 · And nowhere is that more clear than right here.

0:47 · US-19 runs north to south, down Florida’s Gulf Coast and bisects the small community of New Port Richey cutting off its downtown from its coastal features.

0:56 · Which means traveling east to west, or vice versa requires you to cross it.

1:00 · It’s a type of roadway that would feel familiar to Americans.

1:03 · Car culture is visible everywhere from the volume of drivers to the businesses alongside it.

1:10 · And along US-19, drivers are moving fast.

1:13 · The posted speed limit on this stretch is 45 miles per hour.

1:16 · But driving speeds appear to be much faster than that.

1:19 · Traffic safety experts will tell you that speed is one of the most important factors in pedestrian safety.

1:27 · A street design report established that traveling up to 15 miles per hour drivers have a wide peripheral vision.

1:33 · They only need 25 feet to come to a full stop and the risk of fatality if they hit someone is 2%.

1:40 · Once drivers are traveling over 40 miles per hour their peripheral view narrows.

1:45 · They require more room to stop and the risk of fatality climbs to 85%.

1:50 · Enforcing speed limits can only do so much.

1:53 · The built environment, as we call it is sending a message that this is for high speed travel.

2:00 · Robert Schneider led the pedestrian safety study that found that 97% of the roadways with high pedestrian fatalities had multiple lanes.

2:08 · At its widest, US-19 spans 8 lanes which allows cars to pass and move faster than if they were stuck behind another car in a single lane.

2:17 · And the road is straight as an arrow.

2:19 · No curves that would nudge drivers to take it slow.

2:22 · The type of businesses along US-19 support a car-first fast driving environment: Big box stores and strip malls that sit far away from the road with large parking lots in between.

2:32 · And billboards displayed up high for an audience of fast drivers rather than at human scale.

2:38 · Arterial roads like US-19 not quite a street, but not quite a highway were built to keep this high speed traffic off of nearby residential neighborhoods.

2:48 · But this type of sprawling development grew along arterial roads creating a dangerous mix of car centric design with the possibility that pedestrians, cyclists, or public transit users would want to access these business centers.

3:01 · And it explains why arterial roads only make up 13% of US roadways but are the site of 59% of pedestrian deaths.

3:13 · Now, let’s relate that to US-19’s pedestrian design or lack thereof.

3:17 · or… lack thereof.

3:19 · Not everyone can or wants to drive but they still have to get to where they’re going.

3:23 · I walk along US-19 about 3 or 4 times a week, to and from work.

3:27 · It’s a lot cheaper than taking the bus.

3:29 · I was crossing the crosswalk someone was turning and just bumped right into me.

3:35 · I had a few bumps, bruises, you know, some cracked ribs.

3:38 · I have a hearing disability…

3:40 · which causes severe vertigo and issues with balance.

3:45 · So it’s not wise to drive.

3:47 · Every single day…

3:52 · I am…

3:56 · afraid of either getting…

3:58 · bumped or yelled at or honked at or cut off…

4:03 · every day.

4:07 · As a pedestrian trying to cross the road I’d have to choose between this crosswalk…

4:12 · or this one, which is nearly 950 meters away.

4:16 · That’s a 30 or 40 minute walk.

4:18 · A distance so far that it encourages risky jaywalking.

4:21 · There’s a better term for that, it turns out.

4:23 · Cross at a location where there’s no signal.

4:26 · In the profession, we tend to try to say that.

4:28 · Jaywalk is a term that was developed by the auto interests in the early 1900s to essentially shame people who were crossing in the middle of the block which had been okay socially prior to the 1920s, 1930s.

4:46 · The sidewalks are constantly interrupted by the curb cuts into parking lots which introduce more opportunities to interact with a moving car without a signal.

4:53 · I first tried this crosswalk, waited for 10 minutes only to find out it didn’t work, so I tried the next crossing.

5:00 · Robert Schneider told me that the longer you wait at a crosswalk the more pedestrians are incentivized to cross before the signal.

5:07 · Finally, once you do cross you have to traverse the length of the eight lanes…

5:11 · which puts US-19 in the company of 70% of the hot spot roadways in Robert Schneider’s study that force pedestrians to cross five or more lanes.

5:20 · And all of this is so much more treacherous when there is less light.

5:28 · There’s a concept in urbanism called safety in numbers.

5:32 · The more pedestrians there are in an environment, the safer it is to be one.

5:36 · There aren’t many pedestrians along US-19 which makes the high number of fatalities even more alarming.

5:42 · The lower the median household income in a neighborhood the more common it is for pedestrian fatalities to occur there.

5:48 · And that’s because bad street design and arterial roads like US-19 are more likely to exist in those communities.

5:55 · Improving pedestrian design would invite more people to walk making it safer for people who have no other choice.

6:02 · Florida transportation officials are spending millions to improve this stretch of US-19.

6:07 · Like reducing the speed limit, adding more crosswalks adding more lights, and delaying green light to intersections.

6:14 · The mayor of New Port Richey told me he favors adding pedestrian and cyclist bridges here to get people off the road entirely.

6:22 · These are expensive solutions and unpopular among drivers.

6:25 · But not nearly as hard as the long term goal which is undoing decades of car centric design like removing lanes, adding street parking instead and developing retail and housing in parking lots.

6:36 · A built environment that will get more people on foot more drivers to slow down and will save lives.

6:43 · It’s not a quick solution, but something we need to actually be starting to move towards…

6:48 · rather than continuing to build the sprawling development that we know is dangerous.

7:22 · This video is an adaptation of a Vox.com story by reporter Marin Cogan.

7:28 · Local officials and journalists have credited her reporting for raising awareness about pedestrian safety along this deadly stretch of road.

7:36 · I highly recommend you check out her story that I linked in the description below.

7:40 · Thanks so much for watching.

America’s infrastructure is crumbling. What should be prioritized

PBS NewsHour, 04 07, 2021

Video (5:45)
Description

President Biden’s $2.3 trillion infrastructure plan would prioritize transportation, drinking water and broadband projects, among others. It comes after the American Society of Civil Engineers released its 2021 report card, giving the U.S. infrastructure a C-minus. Emily Feenstra, ASCE’s managing director of government relations and infrastructure initiatives, joins William Brangham to discuss.

Introduction to Plan

0:08 · Our William Brangham brings us this look at why America’s infrastructure is in such need of repair.

0:14 · WILLIAM BRANGHAM: The president’s plan includes funding for many infrastructure priorities, more than $600 billion in transportation infrastructure, more than $100 billion for drinking water projects, and more than $100 billion to expand broadband.

0:30 · Just last month, the American Society of Civil Engineers released its 2021 report card, and it gave America’s infrastructure a C-minus.

ASCE Report Card Findings

0:41 · I’m joined now by Emily Feenstra. She is ASCE’s managing director of government relations and infrastructure initiatives.

0:49 · Emily, great to have you on the “NewsHour.”

0:52 · I have to imagine, on one level, for people – for civil engineers like you, this has got to be an incredibly exciting time, when the president proposes a nearly $2 trillion infrastructure bill.

1:03 · But, more seriously, this is meant to address some very serious deficiencies in our country.

1:11 · Could you just give us a snapshot of what your record card tells us?

1:15 · EMILY FEENSTRA, American Society of Civil Engineers: That is an exciting time.

1:31 · At the same time, I am a parent. I would not be happy if my kid brought home a C-minus. So we have a lot of work to do. And we have 11 categories still in that D range. And those are a lot of our legacy systems.

Highest Priority Repairs

1:51 · EMILY FEENSTRA: One thing that we like is really that comprehensive approach.

1:54 · We look at 17 categories of the report card, and it’s really a connected system. So, in a way, our ports are only as good as the roads and the rail that connect to them. At the same time, if you look at those categories and the D’s, there’s like a few that stand out.

2:12 · Our lowest grade and the report card were our transit systems. Our communities across the country are just facing a huge maintenance backlog when it comes to transit, and the pandemic certainly didn’t help that. The agencies have been facing huge revenue declines.

2:28 · And so they were kind of kicked while they were already down. Wastewater utilities, another area where we’re in the D’s. There’s a lot of work we could be doing. Inland waterways is another one, definitely under the radar for most Americans, but that’s how farmers get their goods to market.

2:52 · And that’s something we really need to prioritize.

Defining Infrastructure

3:08 · And Republicans say, no, that’s not what we traditionally think of as infrastructure.

3:13 · I know the American Society tries to be nonpartisan and apolitical in all of this, but do you guys come down on this issue of what is infrastructure and what is not?

But when you’re thinking about where our kids are spending eight or more hours a day, and you look at the number of kids that are in portable classrooms or HVAC systems aren’t updated, there’s a lot of common ground. There are new things in the proposal that might go beyond the 17 categories.

4:03 · But, again, we appreciate that it includes core programs like surface transportation, but also water, the energy grid, inland waterways, and so many of these – these things that go out of sight, out of mind.

4:17 · WILLIAM BRANGHAM: I hear everything that you’re saying about the importance of these projects, but we know that many people look at this and think it’s too much money to spend, a $2 trillion infrastructure bill is too high a price.

The Cost of Inaction

4:31 · What is your response to that?

4:32 · EMILY FEENSTRA: I can absolutely understand how, sometimes, it seems like sticker shock.

4:36 · But what people don’t realize is that we’re already paying. It’s almost like a hidden tax from this gradually declining, deteriorating infrastructure that doesn’t work the way that it should. And we have actually quantified that costs. In addition to the poor grades, we know that it costs American households on average $3,300 a year in personal disposable income.

4:57 · That’s the equivalent of…

4:58 · (CROSSTALK) WILLIAM BRANGHAM: That’s a huge amount of money.

4:59 · EMILY FEENSTRA: Yes, it’s a takeout dinner for a family of four each week. And that’s significant.

5:06 · And it’s things we know intuitively. When the pothole messes with your alignment that you have driven over five or six times on the way to work, when a water main break shuts down a business, when a blackout, as we saw in Texas, you know wreaks havoc, these things cost money. They add up. They make our economy less productive.

5:25 · And I think what – there actually is strong voter support for these investments.

5:31 · They pass in overwhelming margins at the ballot box at the local and state level. And what we need is that strong federal partner that we have been missing.

5:39 · WILLIAM BRANGHAM: All right, Emily Feenstra of the American Society of Civil Engineers, thank you very much for being here.

Transcript

0:00 · intro It seems like every workplace has that one person who swears that the potted spider plant sitting on their desk has an almost magical ability to purify the air in the office.

0:14 · Are they actually onto something?

0:15 · There is evidence to show that plants can remove pollutants from indoor air.

0:19 · But a single potted plant probably won’t go the distance.

0:22 · If you’ve heard that bringing plants into your home or office will improve your indoor air quality, you probably have a study conducted back in 1989 by NASA to thank for that meme.

0:31 · The goal was to test whether a variety of types of indoor plants could be used for air purification, both on Earth and in space.

0:38 · The plants were put into sealed containers, and the air pumped full of chemicals including benzene and formaldehyde.

0:44 · Those chemicals fall under the broader umbrella of volatile organic compounds, or VOCs.

0:50 · Some VOCs are known to cause health issues like headaches or liver and kidney damage.

0:53 · And they’re noteworthy as indoor pollutants because household products and building materials can give them off.

0:59 · The plants were kept under controlled conditions, with plenty of light and water and the air quality was measured over a 24 hour period.

1:06 · The study found the majority of the plants included in the experiment removed much of the benzene and formaldehyde from the containers.

1:11 · Plants are thought to remove pollutants from the surrounding air by absorbing the gases through their leaves and roots with some possible help from the microorganisms in the soil.

1:19 · So that’s it, right?

1:20 · Houseplants help clean the air?

1:21 · Well, not quite.

1:22 · Later studies doing similar experiments have yielded mixed results.

1:26 · A 2009 study tested 28 varieties of indoor plants and found four that were best at capturing every VOC the researchers threw at them.

1:33 · So plants definitely can remove some pollutants in a laboratory test chamber.

1:38 · But these idealized lab conditions don’t exactly represent the air in your office – stuff like the amounts of light, water, and air circulation are all going to be different.

1:47 · On top of that, the lab plants were purifying the air in a small area.

1:52 · Some of the chambers in the NASA study were less than a cubic meter in volume.

1:55 · That means for the same amount of purification to happen in your house, you would need an indoor rainforest.

2:01 · One critic of the NASA study suggested that to get the same effect in a typical home you’d need about 680 separate plants.

2:08 · There have been a handful of other studies investigating the effects of plants on indoor air quality, but at least one review, published in 2014, has attempted to take stock of the existing research.

2:18 · And it concluded that, while lab-based studies generally show some effect, not many have been performed in living spaces, and the ones that have been done haven’t yielded a consensus.

2:26 · So don’t count on your poor desk fern to fix all of your indoor air problems.

2:31 · Thanks for watching this episode of SciShow, and thanks to Emma Hulton for asking.

2:35 · To find out how to maybe get your questions answered, head over to patreon.com/scishow.

2:39 · [ outro ]

Creating Climate-Resilient Communities through Vacant Lot Restoration

National Wildlife, 06 29, 2021

Video (5:36)
Description

Over the last two years, National Wildlife Federation piloted a project with the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society’s Philadelphia LandCare program to transform a network of vacant lots into climate-resilient wildlife habitat. We wanted to explore how cities with vacant lots can restore these sites to provide pollinator habitat, green stormwater infrastructure, equitable access to nearby nature, and create economic/job training opportunities.

Learn more: 1) https://www.nwf.org/Magazines/National-Wildlife/2021/April-May/Conservation/Lot-Revival 2) https://blog.nwf.org/2021/02/vacant-lots-to-pollinator-habitat-in-philadelphia-pa/

0:27 · It It’s making a difference. It’s making an impact in people’s lives.

The land care program

0:34 · The city of Philadelphia is a post-industrial city, and so we have a lot of vacant lots in the city. And unfortunately, most of them, whether they’re privately owned or city-owned, don’t have the capacity to maintain them.

0:47 · And so they grow heavy weeds, and, you know, people dump their trash on there, and there’s debris, and it’s just It’s an eyesore. It’s not something that people deserve to live by.

0:58 · So that’s where we at PHS come in. We have our Philadelphia Land Care program, where we completely clean and green these vacant lots, so that you know, what was formerly a terrible eyesore is now a community asset, which people can use, and people can enjoy, and they feel safer around.

1:17 · Through this project, we’re trying to change the narrative behind vacant lots, and switching it from a detriment and a negative to a community asset, and realizing that we have all this open, accessible land, and that it could serve as easy and equitable access to nature and to green space in urban environments, but it can also provide ecological habitat as well.

Greening and infrastructure

1:42 · We’ve noticed the soil quality has improved, which helps with drainage. And we In Philadelphia, have a lot of of stormwater management issues when it rains heavily.

1:52 · PHS, their Land Care program, they’ll stabilize a lot, and they’ll bring in sod, and they’ll plant some trees, but we are taking this awesome program to the next level, and we’re installing pollinator gardens, um which serve as habitat for birds, bees, and butterflies, and all sorts of critters. These gardens are able to absorb more runoff and stormwater, preventing overflows in sewers. So we’re really hoping that not only can we provide habitat, but we can provide water quality benefits as well.

2:21 · Some of our our lots, we collaborate with the Mural Arts program, which they paint these beautiful murals. And then, the National Wildlife Federation, in collaboration with the a local university, they found that it has a positive impact on the climate, as well.

Art and wildlife impact

2:36 · So when we have the the clean lawn, the mural, and then the added texture and and beauty from the gardens, it really creates such a beautiful space for the community.

Local economic impact

2:49 · We’re also working with 12,000 lots, which is a lot. You can’t manage that much through a volunteer basis. So we found it actually to be much more sustainable by hiring local contractors or working with community organizations to maintain the lot itself. And what’s great is that we actively search to work with local landscape contractors to help build their capacity. And they hire community members from the neighborhoods that we’re that we’re working in.

3:18 · And so really, you know, we’re investing a lot of dollars to clean these lots, but that money’s going right back into the neighborhoods, helping to create jobs, and then it it helps kind of build ownership, as well.

Personal perspective

3:32 · When you get up in the morning, you know, just taking your kids to daycare, school, you want your community to look right. You don’t want to come out, see trash everywhere, or just a mess. I’m only like 30 days, if that, in, but it’s giving me a different perspective on like everything, far as beautifying your neighborhood. Even though it’s a job, when you go back home and you see like a lot on your block when you’re not at work, you’re going to probably want to do something to it, like, why we can’t just make every block and every street in the city look good? Landscaping gave me a a different outlook about life.

4:06 · What landscaping really is not just like weed whacking, cleaning, it’s a whole lot of other aspects that go into it to try to help brighten and raise awareness in different communities. I wanted a contractor to really give me like an opportunity that I never had. I’m here to just get the experience, you know, listen, observe, pay attention to details.

4:27 · You know, there’s a lot of lots that need work, and if you can get a lot of positive people and people to work with you, clean the lots up, it’s a mess in the beginning, but when you step back and look at it with, you know, all the heart for the community, um it’ll weigh much more nice for the neighborhood.

Future expansion goals

4:45 · We would really love to see vacant lot restoration at scale throughout the Mid-Atlantic, and so we are really using this project and this opportunity to learn as much as we can about what has worked and what hasn’t, so that we can really bring this to other cities and make it a stronger priority.

0:00 · Chris Rock: You know what’s so sad, man?

0:00 · You know what’s wild?

0:28 · Once you see it, you won’t be able to unsee it.

0:31 · OK, let’s look at MLK Boulevard in Baltimore.

0:35 · I want to show you how to see housing segregation in schools, in health, in family wealth, in policing.

0:41 · But first, an explanatory comma.

0:45 · It’s the 1930s in the wake of the Great Depression.

0:47 · FDR is president.

0:48 · He wants to bring economic relief to millions of Americans through a collection of federal programs and projects called The New Deal.

0:54 · One part of that “new deal” was The National Housing Act of 1934, which introduced ideas like the 30-year mortgage and low, fixed interest rates.

1:03 · So now you have all these lower-income people who can afford homes, but how do you make sure they don’t default on their new mortgages?

1:09 · Enter the Home Owners Loan Corp.

1:12 · The HOLC created residential security maps.

RESIDENTIAL SECURITY MAPS

1:15 · And these maps? They’re where the term redlining comes from.

1:20 · Green meant “best area, best people,” aka businessmen; blue meant “good people,” like white-collar families; yellow meant a “declining area,” with working class families; and red meant “detrimental influences, hazardous,” like “foreign-born” people, “low-class whites,” and – most significantly – “Negroes.”

1:41 · Again and again on these HOLC maps, one of the most consistent criteria for redlined neighborhoods is the presence of black and

brown people.

1:49 · Let’s be clear.

1:50 · Studies show that people who lived in redlined areas were not necessarily more likely to default on their mortgages.

1:57 · But redlining made it difficult — if not impossible — to buy or refinance.

2:02 · So landlords abandon their properties.

2:04 · City services become unreliable.

2:06 · In most places, crime increases.

2:09 · And property values drop.

2:11 · All of these conditions fester for 30 years as white people flee to the brand new suburbs popping up all over the country.

2:18 · Many of those suburbs institute rules, called covenants, that explicitly forbid selling homes to black people.

2:23 · And all of this was perfectly legal.

2:27 · Now it’s 1968.

2:29 · And MLK is assassinated.

2:31 · News Report: Good evening.

2:32 · The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, 39 years old, The apostle of nonviolence in the civil rights movement has been shot to death in Memphis, Tenn.

2:39 · Martin Luther King was shot and was killed tonight in Memphis, Tenn.

2:42 · In the aftermath, Congress passes the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

2:47 · It’s a policy meant to encourage equal housing opportunities regardless of race, or religion or national origin.

2:52 · And it offers protections for future homeowners and renters, but does little to fix the damage already done.

2:58 · Over the next 50 years, the Fair Housing Act is rarely enforced.

3:02 · So you can still see housing segregation and its effects, in Baltimore and often along any MLK Boulevard in any U.S. city.

3:11 · Like its effects on wealth.

WEALTH

3:13 · So homeownership is the major way Americans create wealth, right?

3:16 · Well, discrimination in housing is the major reason that black families up and down the income scale have a tiny fraction of the family wealth that white families do – even white families with less education and lower incomes.

3:28 · For almost 30 years, 98 percent of FHA loans were handed out to white borrowers.

3:33 · Not only were black neighborhoods redlined, and not only was the Fair Housing Act selectively enforced, if at all, but it is still today much harder for a black person to get a mortgage or home loan than it is for a white person.

3:46 · John: Families are fearful of speaking up about a basic human right that should be afforded to everyone in the world but definitely in the richest country in the world.

3:59 · And housing segregation in schools.

4:02 · The primary way that Americans pay for public schools is by paying property taxes.

4:07 · People who live in more valuable homes have better-funded local schools, better-paid teachers, better school facilities and more resources.

4:15 · Here’s a feedback loop: The better the schools in a neighborhood, the more those homes in that neighborhood are worth.

4:21 · And the higher the property values of those homes, the more money there is for schools.

4:25 · And so on and so on.

4:27 · And housing segregation in health.

4:29 · Because of urban planning that benefited those richer, whiter neighborhoods, people of color are more likely to live near industrial plants that spew toxic fumes; they’re more likely to live far away from grocery stores with fresh food, and in places where

the water isn’t drinkable.

HEALTH

4:43 · They’re more likely to live in neighborhoods with crumbling infrastructure, and in homes with toxic paint.

5:00 · And, not coincidentally, people of color have higher incidences of certain cancers, asthma and heart disease.

5:08 · And housing segregation in policing.

POLICING

5:11 · Housing segregation means we are having vastly different experiences with crime and vastly different experiences with policing.

5:17 · Because our neighborhoods are so segregated, sometimes racial profiling can be camouflaged as spatial profiling — where living in certain areas can make you more likely to be stopped by the police.

5:29 · And it means people have a lot of unnecessary contact with the criminal justice system just because of where they live.

5:38 · Reggie: The problem in our city?

5:41 · The police and the citizens are fighting.

5:43 · They keep targeting my brothers and sisters who don’t really have nothing.

5:49 · And that heavy, aggressive kind of policing that you see in black neighborhoods in particular makes people feel like they can’t trust the police.

5:55 · And when people don’t trust the police, crimes go unsolved and people have to find other ways to keep themselves safe.

6:03 · But, of course, it’s not just Baltimore.

6:05 · Because housing segregation and discrimination fundamentally shape the lives of people in nearly every major American city.

6:14 · It really is in everything.

How “Third Places” Make Cities Healthier, Stronger

Martin Felsen - City Design, 10 02, 2025

Video (7:38)
Description

Cities can boost our health—when we feel like we belong. Explore how “third places” (neither home nor work) turn bricks and mortar into trust, ties, and well-being. From cafés and libraries to community centers and markets, see how everyday spaces compound into social capital—and why some cities now invest in third places first.

Watch to learn: - What “third places” are and why they matter for health and democracy - How small, low-stakes interactions build social capital - Why participation in clubs and associations has declined—and how design can counter it - How social prescribing links people to community groups - The U.S. Industrial Policy playbook: jobs → families → civic groups → trust in third place - The “third-place-first” strategy in cities beyond the U.S. and how quality of place attracts families and jobs - A tour of PILARES in Mexico City—how design + programming drive belonging and well-being - Practical examples of third place programs any city can host today

If you’re enjoying CityDesign, like, subscribe, and share to help more people discover how we shape cities—and how cities shape us.

About me

Martin Felsen, FAIA, co-founded UrbanLab, an architecture and urban design firm in Chicago. Martin is a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects, and a Professor in the Illinois Institute of Technology’s (IIT, aka, Illinois Tech) College of Architecture. UrbanLab’s work synthesizes diverse design methodologies and technical innovations drawn equally from architecture and its complex urban and natural contexts. Built work to date includes houses, housing, mixed-use buildings, installations, and urban infrastructural projects. UrbanLab has received many design awards for projects across scales of production.

Transcript
The decline of civic ties

0:00 · Hi, I’m Martin Felson. Welcome to City Design, the channel where we explore how we shape cities and how cities shape us.

0:08 · Today’s question is, how do cities improve our health and well-being?

0:13 · Cities physically connect us. A first principle of city design is simple. We are not meant to be alone. We do much better when we share purpose in shared places. But today, our civic ties have thinned. Participation in clubs, associations, and congregations is way down. What’s at stake isn’t nostalgia.

0:34 · It’s social capital. The trust, the norms, and networks that help communities solve problems together. Why the decline in our physical connections, familiar forces, mobility uproots us, and screens capture our attention. As an urban designer, I also see an antidote.

The role of third places

0:54 · Brick and mortar third places. These are gathering spots that are neither home nor work. They’re where we swap ideas, organize, and belong. Cafes and barber shops, libraries and schools, faith halls and field houses. Third places normalize low stakes contact, and those weak ties add up to deliver enhanced well-being. They help us connect and cope together. Third places aren’t new.

1:22 · In the 1830s, Alexis Dtoqueville observed that Americans penchant for starting civic associations was a key factor to our unprecedented ability to make democracy work. He wrote that we’re forever forming a thousand different kinds of associations, every kind, large and small. What happens inside third places? They convert bricks and mortar into trust and ties. Physical capital into social capital. Their design matters, too.

How spaces build social capital

1:53 · Open, simple, yet versatile spaces instill a sense of ownership and group pride. Public libraries host book and hobby clubs, free classes, and meetups. Community centers host arts and fitness classes, neighborhood gatherings, and volunteer drives. Parks host walking groups, nature clubs, and community cleanups.

2:18 · City service offices host neighborhood associations, and block clubs. Houses of worship host service groups, support circles, and food pantries. Parishes, JCC’s, YMCA host wreck teams, community service projects, and family programming. Public schools host afterhour PTAs, youth clubs, and adult wreck leagues. Boys and girls clubs host teams, clubs, mentoring, and service projects.

2:48 · Clinics and health centers host mindfulness groups, caregiver classes, and peer support. Food banks host nutrition and cooking classes, and volunteer and service clubs. Maker spaces host hobby clubs, and skill and repair shares. Museums, galleries, and cultural centers host dosan programs, lectures, and arts clubs. Rec centers host leagues, pickup games, and volunteer coaching and referee training.

3:17 · Cafes and bars host book clubs, language tables, and interest group meetups.

3:23 · Co-working spaces host professional associations. Farmers markets host info booths, volunteer signups, and community campaigns. Different places, same effect. Regular contact, small commitments, real purpose. That’s how physical spaces compound into social capital and how social capital strengthens mental health and democratic life. Healthc care is catching up, too.

Policies for healthy cities

3:50 · Doctors and clinicians now use social prescribing, which are patient referrals to groups, classes, and caregivers circles. Because joining a third place group measurably improves our health.

4:03 · More broadly in the US, national public policies focus on jobs, families, and third places as direct paths to citizen and community well-being. Our industrial policy targets business sectors with incentives and penalties to raise job quantity and quality.

4:21 · Stabilizes families with home ownership and good jobs. channels family members into community organizations to spur civic participation, which finally deepens civic trust and well-being through participation in third places abroad.

A third place first strategy

4:40 · Some cities flip the order with a third place first strategy. Build third place social infrastructure. Catalyze networks of people and organizations that undergur local economies. Attract investment in jobs via quality of place.

4:56 · stabilize family and home as civic life strengthens. Let’s look at how this strategy works in practice. Polaris are small community centers cited across Mexico City. These are places to find free computers in internet, flexible classrooms, and hands-on workshops from carpentry to coding. Many include courtyards that flip from classes to festivals to civic meetings. Polaris work because sites are prioritized in underserved areas. Buildings are well-designed and easy to identify.

5:29 · Programs are free and ongoing. In Ketal Kowal, this Polaris offers educational and practical support to rebuild social ties and safety within a dicey neighborhood. Classrooms and workshops open onto a shared courtyard and the operable facade signals that the space is open to all and available for everyday use and community ownership. In ease to Palapa on a tight site with little open space, the entry plaza and column threshold pulls the street inside the Polaris.

Case study: Polaris centers

6:02 · Simple materials, strided block, concrete tile, steel create light, shade and durable rooms that flex from forum to classroom. In qui Quilo, a slender steel frame shades the interior spaces of this neighborhood hub. The inverted roof captures rainwater architecture doing double duty in a water stressed city. In La Pula, this educational center has a single unified room on two levels.

6:31 · The large multi-purpose space offers free training workshops of all kinds for everyone in the neighborhood. In Valentine Gomez FAS, this Polaris is filled with naturally lit classrooms linked to a public walkway with lattice walls and gardens used for learning and neighborhood life. Free classes, workshops, and outdoor forums entice people of all ages to gather, learn, and belong. The bottom line here is that third places aren’t a luxury.

Innovation in belonging

7:01 · They’re our everyday infrastructure of connection and well-being. Design them well. Program them predictably. Open them to everyone. The benefits compound.

7:14 · We talk a lot about innovation in technology. Here’s another kind.

7:18 · Innovation in belonging. Cities that invest in it will be healthier, safer, and more confident about their future.

7:26 · Thanks for watching City Design. If you’re enjoying these episodes, please like, share, and subscribe.

How FIVE BILLION Pounds of Las Vegas Garbage Powers a City

PBS Terra, 04 20, 2021

Video (9:14)
Description

PBS Member Stations rely on viewers like you. To support your local station, go to: http://to.pbs.org/DonateTerra

Celebrate Earth Day with our friends at PBS: https://bit.ly/3elpV1w

Head over to Reactions to find out more about how they’re celebrating Earth Day, and tell them Joe sent you! https://youtu.be/I1YLPfSuNXY

Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites.

One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Because it serves a non-stop city, the landfill must operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It receives upwards of 16 million pounds of trash per day or 5 billion pounds per year.

Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada.

Subscribe to PBS Terra! - https://bit.ly/3mOfd77

Hosted by Joe Hanson from It’s Okay to be Smart, Overview uses incredible 4k drone footage to reveal the natural phenomena shaping our planet from a 10,000-foot view—literally.

Transcript
Intro

0:02 · [Host Joe Hanson] Americans produce 4.9 pounds of waste per person per day. That’s nearly 600 billion pounds per year.

0:11 · Where does it all go?

0:13 · It goes to places like this. The mountains of trash we throw away can have huge impacts on our environment and climate.

0:23 · But what if I told you that all of this waste could one day power a city?

0:29 · [synth music] ♪ [Joe] Welcome to Las Vegas, the place for glitz, glam, gambling and garbage. Three main categories of waste are solid waste, recyclables, and food waste. And here in the neon city, we’re going to explore the ways they’re turning each of these trash types into treasure. Las Vegas produces more than five billion pounds of waste per year, and all that trash ends up here. The Apex Landfill lies in the mountains beyond the city.

Apex Landfill

1:12 · At 1900 acres, it’s one of the largest landfills in North America, and also one of the busiest. Apex is one of the only landfills in North America that runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year. As many as 250 trucks enter the landfill each day and deliver up to 16 million pounds of waste. It used to be a place like this was called a dump, and that’s exactly what they were.

1:46 · trash dumped in piles with little regard for sanitation. As trash decays, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. The dumps of yesteryear all but ignored this, as well as other environmental problems. But today’s landfills are feats of engineering. They are long-term storehouses for society’s garbage and places where we manage its potential hazards.

2:14 · [David Vossmer]: It would be comparable to a construction site, where you’re building homes in a neighborhood. We would envision an entire city being built basically as a landfill.

2:26 · [Joe]: David Vossmer has been working in the solid waste industry for 42 years and oversees operations at Apex.

Working Phase

2:33 · [David]: The working face is the active area of the landfill, usually anywhere from two to three acres in size.

2:41 · [Joe]: Each truck that dumps its load carries about 30 tons of garbage. Compactors then take that trash, spread it across the working face, and mash it down.

2:57 · [David]: Each one of those machines is about 120 to 130,000 pounds. There’s a lot of weight that will smash all the cardboard boxes or trash or any other material that comes in. It’ll lay it down in a nice, even layer. That’s what the landfill business is trying to do, get as much compacted waste into that area or that acre that we can. That’s what extends the life of the landfill.

3:24 · [Joe]: As more and more trash comes in, the landfill grows in height.

3:29 · [David]: It’s just like building a pyramid. The wider the base, the higher we can go with the trash here in the landfill.

3:36 · [Joe]: In some areas, the local landfill is the highest point in the region. Here in Vegas, this mountain of trash is 500 feet high and rising taller by the day. In spite of the enormous volume of garbage coming in, the landfill will be able to take in trash for another 300 plus years.

3:57 · How is that possible?

4:01 · Not only is the site large, but it’s also growing. A mining company on site digs out the surrounding mountains. In the process, it expands the landfill’s footprint and the space it has to operate. But the best way to keep a landfill from filling up is to waste less. Las Vegas boasts the largest residential recycling center in North America. The state-of-the-art facility takes in up to 1.8 million pounds of recyclables per day.

Recycling

4:32 · Because Las Vegas uses single stream recycling, all the sorting happens here. These recyclables will get conveyed through a complex system of sorting machines.

4:45 · [Jeremy Walters]: We have some very unique pieces of equipment, things that do just simple mechanical separation through disks and screens, but we also have computerized machines that are physically reading the material based on its color and density. It’s very smart, and it’s very quick. After a machine initially separates material, people quality control what the machine did.

5:10 · They’re physically looking at the material to ensure that the machine sorted correctly and there are no contaminants within that final product.

5:19 · [Joe]: A new challenge confronting recycling centers like this is the Amazon effect. Facilities around the country are being inundated with cardboard from online retailers. Here at this facility, they’ve had to recalibrate their machines and processes just to handle the deluge. While 1.8 million pounds of daily recyclables might sound like a lot, it’s still just a fraction of the overall waste that gets created each day.

5:49 · Food is another thing that inundates the waste stream and doesn’t belong in a landfill. Las Vegas is renowned buffets produce a lot of it. But here in Sin City, they’ve found an innovative solution. It’s not just people who pig out on buffets. The residents of the Las Vegas Livestock Farm enjoy it too. The farm sits on Apex property, but is family-owned.

6:17 · [Hank Combs]: Hog farming in Nevada is not very popular, because of the access to feed. We’ve circumvented that by doing the food scrap route, which is a very sustainable way to raise our hogs.

6:28 · [Joe]: They take in up to 40,000 pounds per day of the casinos’ food waste. Everything from lobster to ice cream gets processed in giant cookers to make it safe for the hogs to eat. This fragrant stew won’t make the menu in any casino, but it’s irresistible to these hogs.

Food Waste

6:48 · I mean, yummy.

6:50 · [Hank]: They’re a lot like a human, so they love their sweets and their meat and the potatoes. They’re not too big on salads. They won’t eat anything. They’re picky.

7:00 · [Joe]: It’s not just food waste that’s finding a second life in Vegas. The garbage is too. In the U.S., landfills like this account for nearly 20% of the human-caused methane emissions. Some landfills capture and burn it. But here at Apex, and at a growing number of landfills around the country, they’re turning it into energy. 160 wells have been drilled into this mountain of trash, some as deep as 200 feet.

7:31 · The wells siphon off the gas coming from landfill. After it’s purified, it’s sent to an onsite power plant where it’s burned to spin turbines, which create energy. That energy is fed back into the electric grid and powers 11,000 homes here in Southern Nevada. The total amount of energy produced annually by U.S. landfills powers the equivalent of more than 1 million homes.

7:56 · [Jeremy]: We’re actually able to take something that is always going to exist in a landfill, and turn it into something that the community can benefit from. Most people go day to day without thinking about the trash or the recyclables that they make. It’s just a simple toss it in the bin and forget about it.

8:10 · And there’s so much involved behind the scenes to make sure that we are handling all those materials in the most environmentally responsible way.

8:20 · [David]: Not everything in our world is recyclable. And as long as society throws things away, we’re one of the things that take care of making sure it’s done the right way.

8:33 · [Joe]: Hey guys, our PBS friends across YouTube are celebrating Earth Day with us. Follow me over to Reactions to find out why catalytic converters are being stolen from cars worldwide, and what this weird mystery has to do with the health of our environment. Tell them Joe sent you.

8:51 · And one more thing, for those of you in the U.S., you should check out “Greta Thunberg: A Year to Change the World,” a new three-hour Earth Day broadcast event on your local PBS station. The special is going to premiere on Thursday, April 22nd at 8:00 pm, 7:00 pm Central, and will then repeat starting Wednesday, April 28th at 8:00 pm, 7:00 pm Central.

Transcript
Intro

0:01 · This is the largest green roof in New York City.

0:04 · It’s in the middle of bustling Manhattan, on top of the Javits Convention Center— a behemoth of a building with a six-block footprint.

0:13 · But the roof hasn’t always been green.

0:16 · Before 2014, it was totally barren.

0:20 · Now, just a few years later, when people walk out onto the roof, they say things like: “Amazing,” “That’s great,” “I didn’t expect this,” “What a surprise.”

0:28 · But besides the great reactions, there are practical benefits.

0:31 · We have 300,000 bees.

0:34 · We’ve seen 25 different species of birds on the roof.

0:36 · We reduced the temperature up here by about six degrees Fahrenheit.

0:39 · And we also save about 7 million gallons of stormwater runoff that’s absorbed in the soil and the plants that are on our roof.

0:46 · We’ve been able to reduce our energy

consumption by about 26 percent, and that translated for us last year

into a saving of about 3 million dollars.

0:55 · That is impressive.

Green Roofs

0:58 · How does one green roof get so much done?

1:01 · And what are all of the NOT green roofs in New York City doing with their lives?

1:06 · First, let’s see how much roof space actually exists.

1:09 · You know, they are a major part of urban landscapes.

1:12 · The the round number that most of us think exists is about 1 billion square feet.

1:18 · One billion with a ‘b.’

1:20 · That’s like 22 times the size of Central Park, in roofs.

1:24 · And in most cities, what isn’t roof is another impermeable surface like road, sidewalk, or parking

lot.

1:31 · And these surfaces create a lot of problems for cities That green roofs can actually help solve.

stormwater runoff

1:38 · Let’s take a look at three of these issues. The first is

stormwater runoff.

1:42 · Rainwater goes in pipes. It combines

with what’s called sanitary water.

1:48 · When there’s too much rainwater, which happens hundreds of times a year around Manhattan, the wastewater treatment

systems shut down, and valves just let the water just, you know, shunt out into the rivers. You know, it’s got human sewage.

2:01 · It’s the biggest source of pathogens to

the Manhattan Island.

2:04 · With green roofs, that water instead of going into the

drain and polluting the environment, ends up just evaporating the atmosphere

through the leaves of these plants.

heat island effect

2:13 · And then, there’s what scientists call the “heat island effect,” which basically means that cities are significantly warmer than the surrounding areas.

2:20 · I’ve seen asphalt roofs get up easily 170, 180 degrees Fahrenheit in the strong sunlight.

2:26 · They absorb about 90 to 95 percent of the sunlight.

2:30 · Green roofs, by comparison are close to air temperatures.

habitat loss

2:34 · Another problem green roofs can help solve is habitat loss.

2:37 · Cities can shrink or destroy the green space that’s crucial for certain plants and

animals to survive.

2:43 · Currently a lot of species might occur in smaller parks throughout the city that are relatively unconnected, But having high densities of green roofs would allow those patches to be more connected.

2:53 · Letting, for example, butterflies travel from patch to patch with lots of stepping stones of green roofs in between.

2:59 · And these are just three of the problems that green roofs can help solve.

conclusion

3:03 · But to really put a dent in any of these issues cities would have to implement green roofs at a large scale.

3:09 · Stuart Gaffin, the research scientist

you heard from earlier, estimates that if all of New York City’s 1 billion square feet of roof space were greened, those green roofs could lower the city’s

temperature by nearly two degrees Fahrenheit and absorb over 10 billion

gallons of stormwater each year.

3:27 · As cities continue to grow, all that empty roof space starts to look more and more like an opportunity, an untapped resource, a future ecosystem of problem-solving meadows in the sky.

How the US made affordable homes illegal

Vox, 08 16, 2021

Video (9:41)
Description

The rules that keep American housing expensive.

Subscribe and turn on notifications (🔔) so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Over the past year, housing prices in the US rose precipitously. Low interest rates and millennials’ entry into the market spiked demand across the nation, leading housing prices in some cities to increase by more than 20 percent in one year, and crushing the dreams of many would-be homeowners.

But housing prices in the US were a problem long before 2020 — and while demand is a big part of the story, there’s an even bigger reason it’s increasingly difficult for Americans to find affordable housing: We don’t have enough houses. According to one estimate, the US is now facing a nearly four-million-home shortage. And the primary reason for that shortage is what’s called exclusionary zoning.

Zoning laws are the local rules and regulations that decide what types of homes can be built where. These rules can sometimes have good intentions. But they also have a dark history in the United States as a tool to keep certain races, religions, and nationalities out of white neighborhoods. And while zoning laws in the US are no longer explicitly racist, their effect remains basically the same: to keep affordable housing, and the people who need it, away from the wealthiest Americans.

Today, in the majority of the US, especially in cities with good jobs, it’s illegal to build many affordable types of housing. And it’s led to a widespread affordability crisis. Watch the video above for more.

Sources:

Jerusalem Demsas reports on housing policy for Vox, and she’s written a ton about this issue:

Houses are getting more and more expensive. There’s a simple fix for that: https://www.vox.com/22464801/housing-bubble-market-crash-supply-shortage-great-recession

What it’ll take to fix America’s housing rules: https://www.vox.com/22252625/america-racist-housing-rules-how-to-fix

The housing shortage is making discrimination a lot easier: https://www.vox.com/2021/5/26/22453293/housing-supply-shortage-discrimination-real-estate-cover-letters

Why the housing market boomed despite the recession: https://www.vox.com/22264268/covid-19-housing-insecurity-housing-prices-mortgage-rates-pandemic-zoning-supply-demand

The zoning maps in the video came from UC Berkeley’s Othering & Belonging Institute: https://belonging.berkeley.edu/single-family-zoning-san-francisco-bay-area

Freddie Mac: http://www.freddiemac.com/research/insight/20210507_housing_supply.page

US Census Bureau: https://www.census.gov/construction/nrc/historical_data/index.html
