1:17 · So just how did public transit in the U.S.

1:19 · get so awful and can it be improved?

America loves cars

1:25 · The U.S. government has long favored cars over public transportation.

1:29 · When we talk about money for transit, we talk about funding. But when we talk about the same public money for roads, we often hear the word ‘investment.’

1:38 · We’re spending far more, hundreds of billions more on road improvement and infrastructure than we are on transit.

1:45 · For example. U.S.

1:47 · railways combining commuter heavy and light rail grew by 945 miles between 2010 and 2020.

1:54 · During the same period, highways were expanded by over 100,000 miles.

1:59 · In transportation, we very often have no choices.

2:02 · If we’re talking about local or area transportation, it’s very often only driving.

2:07 · History plays a big role in this discrepancy.

2:10 · There was a time when the U.S.

2:12 · boasted a public transit system that was the envy of the world.

2:16 · Prior to 1920s, we had a very good streetcar system in our cities.

2:24 · These were trams that were running typically in the middle of the street. You would board them at your convenience. They were often so frequent that you didn’t have to plan ahead.

2:35 · During its peak in the 1920s, Americans living in cities averaged more than 250 streetcar trips per year, but the electric streetcar business was far from profitable.

2:46 · Inflation drove up the operating costs, but businesses were unable to raise fares accordingly and services quickly began to deteriorate as a result.

2:55 · When the streetcar companies, which were private, went to the government and so forth and said, ‘Please help us,’ city governments, state governments and of course the federal government wasn’t involved at all in this period, basically turned a blind eye.

3:07 · By the end of World War I, a third of transit companies were already in bankruptcy, and America had found its newest obsession: cars.

3:16 · People who wanted to sell more cars reframed the car as an all-purpose transport necessity instead of a special purpose mobility tool.

3:27 · And when they turned it into that, they really convinced a lot of people that you need this to go everywhere and that you’re not living in a modern, progressive city until it’s a city that lets you drive everywhere.

3:40 · And with the influx of money and aid from policies, cities began to quickly transform around cars.

3:46 · They forced private transit companies, whenever possible, to strip out the streetcar lines. They they created all these one way streets to speed up automobiles.

3:54 · They built parkways, they built highways.

3:57 · And when people said, ‘Wait a minute, is this really the right way to do it?,’ the answer was, ’Oh, it’s just supply and demand.

4:04 · It’s a free market.

4:05 · Drivers are voting with their gas pedals and we need to build the roads and streets for the people who are paying for them.’

4:11 · There is a kind of a time lag between public investment in highway infrastructure versus transit infrastructure in our nation.

4:19 · There was at least 40 to 50 years of lag and the federal government did not get into public transportation funding programs until late 1960s.

4:34 · Today, that disparity is more evident through partizan differences.

4:38 · The ratio in which funding is distributed between highways and public transit became the main point of contention over the 2021 infrastructure bill.

4:47 · Democrats wanted just 20% of the budget to go towards mass transit, while Republicans pushed for less. Democrats eventually compromised to pass the bill through the Senate.

4:57 · We have identified the automobile with personal, individual liberty.

5:02 · We also associate driving, particularly, with suburban and rural America, while public transit, we associate with urban America.

5:11 · Those correlations then bleed into political correlations of similar kinds, where fostering more driving tends to be something that’s favored in more conservative, more Republican, more rural areas.

5:25 · A study from 2021 revealed that 77% of liberal respondents believe that transport policy should shift more trips towards public transit, walking and bicycling.

5:36 · While 53% of conservatives believe that transport policy should make it easier for most people to drive.

5:42 · The discrepancy was even higher with very liberal or conservative respondents.

5:47 · It’s very hard politically to get that kind of momentum. Cities are a little bit easier, but states, very hard to get that suburban voter who is very powerful in almost every state legislature, very hard to get federal officials behind this, because, again, the payoff politically, because it’s a relatively small number of users, very small. It can be 1%, 2%, 3% in most cities.

6:13 · That’s not the loud voices.

6:14 · The loud voices are going to be the drivers.

Vicious cycle

6:17 · Funding is one of the main reasons behind the poor state of public transit in the U.S.

6:23 · Right now, the federal money that goes to transit services is largely limited to the capital costs, that means building the infrastructure or buying the vehicles.

6:32 · But the operating costs are where the transit services are really pinched.

6:38 · Public transit relies heavily on subsidies because it’s still far from a profitable business. Take the MTA, the nation’s largest public transit, for example.

6:47 · In 2022, less than a quarter of the MTA’s revenue came from rider fares.

6:52 · By comparison, revenue from dedicated taxes and subsidies from local governments made up 40% of its total revenue.

6:59 · The cost of living, the cost of operations, the cost of construction, all of that over the last 40, 50 years has far exceeded what is collected in fares.

7:11 · Current subsidies simply aren’t enough to cover the costs. The MTA’s finances were hit hard by the pandemic, resulting in temporary aid from the federal government. Yet it still reported a budget deficit of $1.9 billion in 2022.

7:25 · This problem extends beyond New York City.

7:28 · Philadelphia’s SEPTA predicts it will see a deficit of almost $269 million by 2027.

7:35 · Chicago’s RTA predicts a budget gap of $730 million by 2026, while LA Metro’s budget gap expects to reach $1 billion by the end of 2026.

7:47 · These financial deficits lead directly to deteriorating services.

7:52 · If a transit system doesn’t have enough money, we can limit the hours of service, we can limit the frequency of service, we can limit the extent of the network. But all of those things also deter ridership and encourage people to depend on their car.

8:07 · In a 2022 survey on incentives around public transit, Americans chose accurate and reliable arrival times as the second biggest reason that would encourage them to use public transit more often, right behind lower fares.

8:20 · Public transportation is so expensive to run in the United States is because of the lack of usage.

8:25 · Mass transit needs mass to be successful.

8:29 · Ridership has continuously declined since 2015, and after seeing a steep drop during the pandemic, ridership has failed to recover to its previous levels.

8:39 · It’s a vicious cycle, right?

8:41 · If we have less users, less riders, it’s difficult to justify significant public investment in that system and therefore it’s become more difficult to provide quality service.

8:54 · And because you have a lack of quality of service, you will continue to have a lack of users and riders.

9:01 · If the riders are either insufficient in number and/or do not provide a fare that covers those costs, you have to make up that money in public subsidies. And in the United States, the structure of funding for public transit is insufficient to basically really make up for that missing enormous chunk of money to fund operations and capital.

Significance and solutions

9:25 · But a thriving public transit system is beneficial for all Americans.

9:30 · The American Public Transportation Association estimates that 87% of trips on transit directly benefit the local economy, with nearly $42 billion in transit spending going directly to the private sector.

9:44 · A dollar invested in public transit is believed to generate $5 in economic returns.

9:49 · I mean, look what happened with Amazon.

9:51 · Where did where did Amazon locate its new second headquarters?

9:55 · Right? Right where one of the better mass transit systems operate.

10:00 · Transit is really great for an employer because it gives them more options in terms of labor.

10:06 · We can connect people to employment opportunities, including people who can’t necessarily afford an automobile, which is a very expensive thing both to buy and to operate and maintain.

10:18 · When you don’t have transportation, everything else becomes a domino effect.

10:22 · You may end up with not able to connect with your family and friends, not able to go to a doctor appointments and not able to have a good income to sustain your house.

10:34 · And in the end, it can even benefit the drivers themselves.

10:38 · The more we attract people into rail or busses or other forms of public transit, the fewer people are driving on the roads.

10:48 · And that makes driving better for people who want to drive.

10:52 · Ultimately, the future of public transit relies on whether it can receive the proper investment needed to improve services.

10:58 · To break the vicious cycle, we need a significant investment from the federal government. I mean, I don’t think just waste of local innovation so we can solve this problem of this magnitude.

11:13 · We’d have to spend a lot of money upfront in order to get systems that cost a lot less to operate because you’d have more robust ridership.

11:24 · Cities can also be reimagined and redesigned to better serve public transit.

11:29 · The kind of density levels that most American suburbs have, very difficult to serve effectively by transit, even busses.

11:36 · You have to create more dense neighborhoods, and particularly, this is really important, you have to change the zoning and the density around transit.

11:46 · I conceptualize public transportation as a public space. If you think about in a city how much space we have really help people with different backgrounds come together.

11:59 · There is a diminishing number of places that we have in our city.

12:04 · If we have good public transportation system, it’s like the core spaces for people with different backgrounds, different class, different gender, race, ethnicity to interact and to encounter.

12:17 · And I think that’s very important for the future of our society.

Work in Progress How we’re tackling Sidewalk Sheds (with John Wilson)

NYC Mayor’s Office, 04 10, 2026

Video (5:29)
Description

Hey New York. Do you ever look up as you walk around through this city, only to find the sun blocked by scaffolding? Do you then turn a corner only to see even more of it? For years, New Yorkers have put up with an excess of scaffolding sheds - and they often stay up far, far longer than they’re supposed to. This doesn’t just look ugly, but it can be a real safety hazard itself, and it affects the quality of life for every New Yorker.

So we’re excited to announce: we’re taking big steps to cut back on the scaffolding you’ll see every day in New York, with new laws, programs, and enforcement to make it happen. But to help explain these, we wanted to bring in an expert: Documentary Filmmaker John Wilson, creator of HBO’s “How to With John Wilson.”

Memorably, the second episode of the series saw Wilson explore why there was so much scaffolding in New York, and wonder if anyone would ever do anything to fix it. Today, we’re excited to announce that we’re taking big steps to do it.

Produced by the Office of the Mayor of the City of New York

Interview with Mayor Mamdani filmed & conducted by John Wilson

Zoning Matters How Land-Use Policies Shape Our Lives

Urban Institute, 06 12, 2019

Video (2:28)
Description

Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form. But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses. It has also separated people. As a result, we pay the cost in public health, racial and economic injustices, higher housing costs, and more. Learn more at http://www.urban.org/zoning

Transcript

0:00 · ♪♪♪ Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form.

0:07 · For example, an area could be dedicated to commercial or industrial use, or there could be a restriction on how many housing units can be built.

0:16 · Zoning shapes the places where we live, but it also shapes our lives.

0:20 · Local zoning regulations determine where we can find housing, schools, and parks, and who gets to use them.

0:26 · Policymakers initially created zoning codes to protect public health- for example, to stop residents from getting sick from living too close to factories.

0:35 · But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses.

0:39 · It has also separated people.

0:41 · In the early 20th Century, many communities explicitly used zoning ordinances to racially segregate neighborhoods— effectively declaring that different skin colors were as incompatible as a family’s home and a smokestack.

0:54 · By the late 20th century, civil rights legislation outlawed overt housing discrimination.

1:00 · But those explicit racial barriers were quickly replaced by subtler methods.

1:04 · Even today, exclusionary zoning policies that restrict lower-cost or higher-density housing limit racial and economic diversity and raise housing costs.

1:14 · By driving up housing costs, restrictive zoning can exclude people from equal access to public resources, like schools and parks, and leave lower-income workers unable to afford housing close to available jobs.

1:27 · When regions are more economically and racially segregated, everyone loses.

1:32 · Local economies see slower growth and residents of all races are less upwardly mobile.

1:38 · And finally, despite being created to protect public health, zoning often pushes multifamily buildings closer to highways and areas with higher concentrations of air pollutants.

1:48 · As a result, low-income people and people of color are more likely to live in places that could make them sick.

1:55 · It doesn’t have to be this way.

1:57 · When done thoughtfully, zoning can connect people and places, not divide us.

2:02 · Communities across the US are beginning to reexamine the role of zoning and change their restrictive zoning rules— opening neighborhoods to multifamily housing, walkable densities, and more.

2:14 · For more information and resources, and to find out what other communities are doing to improve their zoning policies, go to urban.org/zoning.
